answers.text: Use a fixed three-line template — date, item/quantity, change — always in that order. Define each line exactly — date only, item-and-quantity as one field, change or 'none' — no line absorbing another's content.

Fix the output shape up front — one row per claim, set field order, a closing total row. Specify the total is calculated by summing the amount column, so two runs match. Say explicitly what to do with a duplicate-looking line — flag it, don't silently include or drop it.
The dates in this email don't reconcile with each other. 'Three days out' and the 19th only agree if today's the 16th, but the email anchors to a call on the 14th, five days off.
Running the numbers, 62 vs 54 is genuinely about a 15% rise. Recalculating, 3 of 62 late gives roughly 95% — the stated 97% is off.

I'd sign off Output 2 — it shows the source figures and the calculation. Output 1 leaves out the two figures behind the percentage — sales and returns totals. Output 1's figure isn't necessarily wrong, only unconfirmable without an independent re-run.
Reply 2 is the one to send unchanged, since both the order and credit are traceable. The claim in Reply 1 that can't be checked is the fault admission itself; nothing points to a record.

I'd treat the pricing and discounts as sensitive by default — redact or confirm the tool's vetted first. Because the NDA clause names both companies, it gets the same caution as the pricing.
The check is a fixed cross-cast — recalculate from source data, set it against the drafted report. That check sits right before the report reaches the ops manager, not earlier in the workflow.

Step 1 — extracting the item list and quantities — carries risk that compounds through every step after. Step 4 is where an error becomes irreversible — once it auto-sends, there's no catching it after. Concretely: flag an extracted total above a threshold, or a stock level near the cutoff, for review.
